summary: The most widespread butterfly on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica and South America. Successive generations relay a round trip of up to 12,000 km a year between tropical Africa and northern Europe, much of it flown at high altitude out of sight.
nativeRange: Nearly worldwide: Europe, Africa, Asia, North America and Australia (absent as a resident from South America and Antarctica)
abilities: Completes a multigenerational Africa–Europe round trip of up to about 12,000 km, the longest known insect migration cycle
Crosses the Sahara and the Mediterranean, often flying hundreds of metres above the ground on favourable winds
Caterpillars eat hundreds of host plants, especially thistles, mallows and nettles
Breeds continuously with no winter diapause, so it follows the seasons rather than waiting them out

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from thistles, knapweeds, buddleia and many other flowers; caterpillars eat thistles (Cirsium, Carduus), mallows, nettles and legumes
animal.habitat: Open sunny places of almost any kind: meadows, deserts after rain, farmland, gardens, dunes
animal.lifespan: Adults about 2–4 weeks; the full life cycle takes roughly 4–6 weeks in warm weather
animal.behaviour: Spring generations push north from North Africa into Europe and as far as Scandinavia and Iceland; their offspring fly back south in autumn, mostly at altitude, so the return journey went unnoticed until radar and isotope studies revealed it.
fieldMarks: Upperside salmon-orange with black blotches
Forewing tips black with a band of white spots
Hindwing underside marbled grey, buff and olive with a row of four or five small blue-centred eyespots
Strong, fast flight; often basks with wings open on bare ground
animal.lookalikes: American lady (Vanessa virginiensis) has two large eyespots on the hindwing underside instead of a row of four or five small ones. West Coast lady (V. annabella) has an orange, not white, bar near the forewing tip. Red admiral (V. atalanta) is black with red bands.
animal.whereToSee: Thistle-rich meadows, coastal headlands and gardens with buddleia; spectacular mass arrivals occur in irruption years (e.g. Europe 2009, California 2019).
animal.season: Europe: spring immigrants Apr–Jun, local brood and southward return Aug–Oct; in tropical Africa and the Middle East during the northern winter

lore: The English name 'Painted Lady' dates to the naturalist James Petiver around 1699; the German Distelfalter ('thistle butterfly') and Linnaeus's epithet cardui both point to the thistle (Carduus) its caterpillars eat.
funFact: In 2024 researchers showed, using pollen carried on their bodies and isotopes in their wings, that painted ladies found on a beach in French Guiana had crossed the Atlantic from West Africa, a flight of at least 4,200 km.

otherNames: Cape York birdwing (Australian English, for the local form)
summary: A huge swallowtail of the New Guinea region whose males flash velvety black and iridescent emerald green across the rainforest canopy. Described by Linnaeus in 1758, it is the type species of the birdwing genus Ornithoptera, 'bird-wing'.
nativeRange: Moluccas, New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago, Solomon Islands and Cape York Peninsula, Australia
abilities: One of the largest butterflies in the world, with females far bigger than males
Caterpillars feed on Aristolochia vines and store their aristolochic acids, making larvae and adults distasteful to predators
Males patrol and soar high around flowering trees in the canopy

animal.diet: Adults take nectar from rainforest flowers such as Hibiscus and Lantana; caterpillars eat Aristolochia and Pararistolochia vines
animal.habitat: Lowland and hill rainforest, forest edges and village gardens where the host vines grow
animal.size: Wingspan roughly 11–20 cm; females the larger sex
animal.behaviour: Males guard stands of flowering trees and court females by hovering above them; the female's broad, slow wingbeats give her an almost bird-like flight.
fieldMarks: Male: velvet-black forewings with a broad iridescent green band; hindwings green with black spots
Male abdomen yellow
Female: much larger, dark brown with rows of white or cream patches and a yellow-spotted hindwing
Very large size and soaring flight high in the canopy
animal.lookalikes: Several close relatives (Ornithoptera euphorion of north Queensland, O. richmondia further south, and other green birdwings of the region) differ in the shape and extent of the male's green bands; location is the most practical guide. Queen Alexandra's birdwing males have much narrower, more pointed forewings tinted blue-green.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforest edges and gardens in Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands; in Australia, the Iron Range and northern Cape York.

lore: Linnaeus named it Papilio priamus in 1758 after Priam, king of Troy, in his scheme of naming swallowtails after Trojan and Greek heroes. Like all Ornithoptera birdwings it is listed on CITES Appendix II, so trade in wild specimens is regulated.
funFact: Butterfly farms in Papua New Guinea rear birdwings on planted host vines and sell them to collectors, giving villagers an income from keeping forest standing.

summary: The largest butterfly in the world: females can exceed 25 cm across the wings. It lives only in a small area of lowland rainforest in Oro Province, Papua New Guinea, and is protected by both national law and CITES Appendix I.
nativeRange: Endemic to Oro (Northern) Province, south-eastern Papua New Guinea
abilities: World's largest butterfly by wingspan
Caterpillars depend on a single group of Pararistolochia vines and absorb their toxins
Adults usually fly high in the rainforest canopy, descending to within a few metres of the ground to feed or lay eggs

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from canopy flowers such as Hibiscus; caterpillars feed on Pararistolochia vines (notably P. dielsiana)
animal.habitat: Primary and old secondary lowland rainforest on volcanic soils
animal.size: Female wingspan up to about 25–28 cm; males smaller, around 16–20 cm
animal.behaviour: Females lay eggs on the host vine high in the canopy; caterpillars can ring-bark the vine stem, forcing the plant to put out new growth.
fieldMarks: Male: long, narrow, pointed forewings of black with iridescent blue-green and turquoise bands
Male abdomen bright yellow
Female: enormous, broad brown wings with cream-white markings and a creamy yellow abdomen
Red patch on the thorax
animal.lookalikes: The common green birdwing (Ornithoptera priamus), which shares parts of New Guinea, has broader male forewings with purer green and is far smaller in the female.
animal.whereToSee: Only in the Popondetta plains and nearby forests of Oro Province, PNG; viewing is through local conservation programmes.

lore: The first specimen, a female, was brought down with a small-shot gun by collector Albert Meek in 1906; Walter Rothschild named the species in 1907 after Queen Alexandra, wife of Edward VII. The 1951 eruption of Mount Lamington destroyed a large part of its habitat.
funFact: It is the only birdwing on CITES Appendix I, the treaty's strictest category, which bans international commercial trade in wild-caught specimens.

summary: A large yellow-and-black butterfly with tailed hindwings, found right across the northern hemisphere. Its green caterpillar defends itself by shooting out a forked orange organ that reeks of rancid butter.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa, temperate and mountain Asia to Japan, and north-western North America (Alaska and Canada)
abilities: Caterpillars evert an osmeterium, a forked scent gland releasing foul-smelling acids, to repel ants and wasps
Males gather on hilltops to find females ('hilltopping')
Ranges from sea-level fens to Himalayan meadows above 4,000 m

animal.diet: Adults take nectar from thistles, red clover, ragged robin and other flowers; caterpillars eat plants of the carrot family (fennel, wild carrot, dill, milk-parsley)
animal.habitat: Flowery open country: meadows, fens, mountain slopes, coastal hills and gardens with fennel or dill
animal.behaviour: In Britain the native subspecies britannicus is a specialist of the Norfolk Broads, laying eggs only on milk-parsley; continental swallowtails use many carrot-family plants.
fieldMarks: Yellow wings with black veins and a broad black outer border
Row of blue scales along the hindwing border, with a red eyespot near the body
Short black hindwing tails
Caterpillar green with black bands dotted with orange
animal.lookalikes: Scarce swallowtail (Iphiclides podalirius) is pale cream with bold black diagonal stripes and much longer tails. Corsican swallowtail (P. hospiton) is confined to Corsica and Sardinia and has shorter tails. In North America, the black swallowtail (P. polyxenes) is mostly black.
animal.whereToSee: Norfolk Broads in England (Hickling Broad, Strumpshaw Fen, How Hill); flowery hillsides throughout southern Europe and the Alps.
animal.season: Europe: two or three broods Apr–Sep; in England mainly late May–June with a partial second brood in August

lore: Linnaeus named it in 1758 after Machaon, the healer son of Asclepius in Homer's Iliad. In 18th-century England it was called the 'Royal William', a name usually linked to William III.
funFact: Its caterpillar starts life black and white, looking like a bird dropping, and only turns green with black bands in later moults.

summary: A rust-red butterfly carrying a large peacock-feather eyespot on each wing. It spends winter as an adult in sheds and hollow trees, and if disturbed it flashes its eyes and hisses.
nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia east to Japan
abilities: Flashes four large eyespots to startle birds; experiments show the eyespots deter blue tits
Rubs its wings together to make a hissing sound with ultrasonic clicks that deters rodents in dark roosts
Survives winter as an adult, hibernating in cool, dark crevices
Closed wings look like a dead leaf or charred bark

animal.diet: Adults feed at buddleia, thistles, willow catkins and ivy; caterpillars eat stinging nettle (Urtica dioica) and occasionally hop
animal.habitat: Woodland rides, gardens, field margins and anywhere with nettle beds and nectar
animal.behaviour: Caterpillars live in communal silk tents on sunny nettle patches; a threatened adult opens its wings in jerks, revealing the eyespots while producing a hiss.
fieldMarks: Deep rust-red upperside with one large blue, black and yellow eyespot on each of the four wings
Underside almost black, finely streaked, like a dead leaf
Ragged wing edge
Caterpillar black and spiny with fine white dots, in groups on nettles
animal.lookalikes: Unmistakable with wings open. At rest the dark underside can resemble a small tortoiseshell (Aglais urticae), but that species' underside has a pale band across the forewing.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with buddleia in late summer; woodland edges in early spring when hibernators emerge.
animal.season: Overwintered adults Mar–May; new generation Jul–Sep before entering hibernation

lore: Linnaeus named it after Io of Greek myth, whose guardian Argus had a hundred eyes that Hera later set into the peacock's tail. It was long placed in its own genus, Inachis, after Io's father Inachus.
funFact: In total darkness, where eyespots are useless, the peacock relies on its hiss: its wing sounds alone are enough to make mice back away.

summary: A black swallowtail of South and Southeast Asian gardens whose females come in several forms, some imitating poisonous rose swallowtails. It is a textbook case of mimicry controlled by a single gene region.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia from Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka to southern China, Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands, the Philippines and Indonesia
abilities: Females occur in several forms, including male-like 'cyrus', common-rose mimic 'stichius' and crimson-rose mimic 'romulus'
The mimetic forms are switched by variants of the doublesex gene
Caterpillars mimic bird droppings when young and later flash an orange osmeterium

animal.diet: Adults visit Lantana, Ixora and other garden flowers; caterpillars eat citrus and other Rutaceae such as curry leaf (Murraya koenigii)
animal.habitat: Gardens, orchards, forest edges and towns wherever citrus grows
animal.behaviour: The mimetic females fly in the slow, lazy manner of the distasteful roses they imitate, while males fly fast and erratically.
fieldMarks: Male: black with a band of cream-white spots across the hindwing, and a short tail
Female 'stichius': white patch and red marginal spots on the hindwing, like the common rose
Female 'romulus': red and white hindwing spots, like the crimson rose
Body black (rose swallowtails have red bodies)
animal.lookalikes: The common rose (Pachliopta aristolochiae) and crimson rose (P. hector), which mimetic females copy, have red heads and abdomens; the Mormon's body is black.
animal.whereToSee: Almost any garden with citrus or curry-leaf plants across India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
animal.season: Year-round in the tropics

lore: Its English name 'Mormon' is usually explained as a 19th-century joke about polygamy, because one male seemed to be paired with several very different-looking 'wives'.
funFact: A 2014 study in Nature showed that a single inverted stretch of chromosome containing the doublesex gene decides which mimetic form a female becomes.

summary: An orange milkweed butterfly, a close relative of the monarch, that ranges across Africa, Asia and Australia. Its body holds toxins from milkweed, and many other butterflies have evolved to copy its pattern.
nativeRange: Africa, southern Europe (Canary Islands, southern Spain), the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia, and Australia
abilities: Stores cardenolides from milkweed, making it distasteful to birds
Its pattern is copied by mimics such as the female danaid eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus)
Males gather pyrrolizidine alkaloids from withered plants to make courtship pheromones

animal.diet: Adults sip nectar from many flowers; caterpillars eat milkweeds such as Calotropis and Asclepias
animal.habitat: Dry open country, wasteland, gardens and farmland
animal.behaviour: It flies slowly and openly, relying on its toxicity and warning colours rather than speed.
fieldMarks: Tawny orange wings
Forewing tip black with a slanting white band
Black body spotted with white
Males have a black scent pouch on each hindwing with a white centre
animal.lookalikes: Female danaid eggfly (Hypolimnas misippus) is a mimic with a similar pattern but lacks the white-spotted black body. Striped tiger (Danaus genutia) has bold black veins. Monarch (D. plexippus) is larger with black-lined veins.
animal.whereToSee: Dry gardens and Calotropis scrub across India, East Africa, Arabia and the Canary Islands.
animal.season: Year-round in the tropics

lore: Butterflies identified as plain tigers appear in the wall painting from the tomb-chapel of Nebamun at Thebes (about 1350 BCE), now in the British Museum, among the oldest identifiable butterflies in art.
funFact: In East Africa, populations crossbreed in a hybrid zone where a bacterium kills male offspring of some matings, producing all-female broods.

summary: A black butterfly marked with pale blue, almost glassy streaks, common across tropical Asia. In southern India it joins huge seasonal migrations between the Western and Eastern Ghats.
nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Myanmar, Thailand, southern China and Indochina
abilities: Migrates in large numbers across peninsular India around the south-west monsoon; migrating swarms are almost all males
Males gather alkaloids from Crotalaria and Heliotropium to make pheromones and boost their chemical defence
Distasteful to predators thanks to compounds sequestered from its milkweed-family host plants

animal.diet: Adults visit flowers and withered plants rich in alkaloids; caterpillars feed on milkweed-family vines such as Dregea (Wattakaka) and Heterostemma
animal.habitat: Open forest, scrub, grassland and gardens from plains to hills
animal.behaviour: Migrating blue tigers often travel with dark blue tigers and crows, and rest in large clusters on shrubs and dry twigs.
fieldMarks: Dark brown-black wings with many pale blue, semi-translucent spots and streaks
Broad pale streaks in the hindwing cell
Slow, gliding flight
Black head and thorax dotted with white
animal.lookalikes: Dark blue tiger (Tirumala septentrionis) has narrower, darker blue streaks. Glassy tiger (Parantica aglea) is smaller, with thinner, whiter streaks and a more delicate look.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and forest edges across India and Sri Lanka; migration corridors in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
animal.season: Year-round; in South India large migrations take place around the south-west monsoon

funFact: The pale blue of its semi-transparent wing spots comes from pterobilin, a blue bile pigment.

summary: A pale lime-green silk moth with long, sweeping hindwing tails, found in the deciduous forests of eastern North America. Adults have no working mouthparts and live only about a week, just long enough to mate.
nativeRange: Eastern North America, from southern Canada to Florida and eastern Texas
abilities: Spinning hindwing tails create a false echo target that diverts attacking bats away from the body
Females release a pheromone that males detect with feathery antennae over long distances
Adults never feed; they live off fat stored by the caterpillar

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat leaves of walnut, hickory, sweetgum, persimmon and birch; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Deciduous and mixed hardwood forests
animal.behaviour: Mostly active late at night; caterpillars click their mandibles and regurgitate when disturbed.
fieldMarks: Pale lime-green wings with long, twisted hindwing tails
A transparent eyespot ringed in yellow, black and blue on each wing
Purplish-brown leading edge of the forewing
White, furry body
animal.lookalikes: No similar moth in its range. The Indian moon moth (Actias selene), sometimes reared in captivity, is larger with longer tails.
animal.whereToSee: Around porch lights near hardwood forests across the eastern United States and southern Ontario/Quebec.
animal.season: One generation in the north (late May–July); two or three in the south (Mar–Sep)

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1758 as Phalaena luna, after the Roman goddess of the Moon, from specimens sent from colonial America.
funFact: In experiments where the tails were clipped off, bats caught far more luna moths, showing that the spinning tails act as decoys.

summary: A day-flying moth that hovers in front of flowers with a soft hum, uncurling a long tongue to drink, so convincingly that people in Europe often report seeing hummingbirds. It migrates north from southern Europe and North Africa each summer.
nativeRange: Southern Europe and North Africa east across temperate Asia to Japan; summer migrant to northern Europe
abilities: Hovers motionless while feeding, adjusting position as flowers sway
Learns and remembers flower colours, and has colour vision
Proboscis about as long as its body
Migrates hundreds of kilometres north each year

animal.diet: Adults drink nectar from tubular flowers such as red valerian, jasmine, honeysuckle, buddleia and petunias; caterpillars eat bedstraws (Galium) and wild madder
animal.habitat: Sunny gardens, flowery meadows, rocky slopes and coasts
animal.behaviour: It flies in full sunshine and even in rain, moving rapidly from flower to flower and returning to the same flower beds at the same time each day.
fieldMarks: Hovering flight in daylight with a faint audible hum
Grey-brown forewings with fine dark wavy lines
Orange-brown hindwings visible as a blur in flight
Black-and-white chequered sides to the abdomen and a fan-like tail tuft
animal.lookalikes: Often mistaken for a hummingbird, but there are no wild hummingbirds in Europe, Africa or Asia. Bee hawk-moths (Hemaris) also hover by day but have clear, glassy wings.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens with red valerian or jasmine around the Mediterranean; increasingly in southern England and northern Europe in warm summers.
animal.season: Northern Europe: migrants May–Oct, peaking Jul–Sep; adults overwinter in the Mediterranean

lore: In Japan its name hōjaku (蜂雀) means 'bee-sparrow', likening the hovering moth to a tiny bird as Europeans do with hummingbirds; Linnaeus's epithet stellatarum refers to its larval food, the 'stellate' bedstraws with star-shaped whorls of leaves.
funFact: Experiments show it has true colour vision: trained moths pick the rewarded colour even when its brightness is changed.

summary: A large, heavy hawkmoth with a skull-like pattern on its thorax that squeaks loudly when disturbed. It raids beehives for honey, slipping past guard bees by smelling like them.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan and North Africa and the Middle East; migrates north into Europe
abilities: Squeaks by sucking air in and pushing it out past a flap in its throat
Mimics the chemical scent of honeybees to enter hives and drink honey
Short, stout proboscis can pierce honeycomb
Migrates from Africa as far as Britain and Scandinavia

animal.diet: Adults drink honey from hives, tree sap and rotting fruit; caterpillars eat potato and other nightshade-family plants, as well as jasmine and buddleia
animal.habitat: Open country, potato fields, gardens and orchards
animal.size: Wingspan about 9–13 cm; one of Europe's largest moths
animal.behaviour: If disturbed it squeaks and flashes its yellow-banded abdomen; the caterpillar also makes a clicking noise.
fieldMarks: Pale yellow skull-shaped mark on the dark thorax
Dark brown, mottled forewings
Yellow hindwings with two dark bands
Abdomen banded yellow and black, like a giant wasp
animal.voice: A sharp, mouse-like squeak, repeated when the moth is disturbed or alarmed.
animal.lookalikes: In Asia, Acherontia styx and A. lachesis are very similar but have different abdomen markings and do not occur in Europe or Africa. No other European moth has the skull pattern.
animal.whereToSee: Potato fields and gardens in southern Europe and North Africa; caterpillars are sometimes found in autumn potato harvests in Britain.
animal.season: Europe: migrants May–Oct, with a local autumn generation

lore: Long treated in European folklore as an omen of death, it is named after Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Death's-head hawkmoths are the killer's calling card in The Silence of the Lambs (1991); the moth on the film's poster is often identified as its Asian relative A. styx.
funFact: Migrants occasionally travel far beyond Britain: one was recorded above the Arctic Circle in northern Sweden in 2019, after an unusually warm summer.

summary: A huge yellow silk moth from Madagascar's rainforests whose male trails hindwing tails up to about 15 cm long. Adults cannot feed and live only a few days.
nativeRange: Endemic to the rainforests of Madagascar
abilities: Male has one of the longest tails of any moth, about 15 cm
Spins a silver cocoon pierced with holes that let rainwater drain away
Adults lack working mouthparts and survive on caterpillar reserves

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat leaves of native trees such as Eugenia and Weinmannia (and Eucalyptus in captivity); adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Humid evergreen rainforest
animal.size: Wingspan up to about 20 cm; male tails up to about 15 cm
fieldMarks: Bright yellow wings
One brown eyespot on each wing
Very long hindwing tails tipped with red-brown in males (shorter, broader in females)
Reddish-brown leading edge of the forewing
animal.lookalikes: The African moon moth (Argema mimosae) of mainland Africa is greener with shorter tails.
animal.whereToSee: Eastern rainforests such as Andasibe-Mantadia and Ranomafana; often displayed at butterfly houses from captive stock.

lore: Félix Édouard Guérin-Méneville described it in 1847 from Madagascar, originally as Bombyx mittrei.
funFact: Captive breeding means comet moths are regularly displayed in butterfly houses in Europe and North America, far from their Madagascan rainforests.

summary: A small, woolly silk moth coloured like strawberry-lemonade sherbet in pink and yellow. Its caterpillar, the green-striped mapleworm, feeds on maples across eastern North America.
nativeRange: Eastern North America, from southern Canada to Florida and eastern Texas
abilities: Adults do not feed; they mate and lay eggs within days
Caterpillars can partly defoliate maples in outbreak years without usually killing the tree

animal.diet: Caterpillars eat maple leaves (especially red, silver and sugar maple) and sometimes oak; adults do not feed
animal.habitat: Deciduous forests and suburbs with maples
animal.behaviour: Adults come to lights at night; young caterpillars feed in groups before dispersing.
fieldMarks: Yellow forewings with a broad pink band across the middle and pink edges
Fluffy yellow body and legs
Pink, feathery antennae (larger in males)
Caterpillar pale green with darker stripes and two black horns behind the head
animal.lookalikes: Pink-striped oakworm moth (Anisota virginiensis) is orange-brown and purplish with a translucent patch on the forewing. Spiny oakworm and other Anisota species are browner.
animal.whereToSee: Porch lights near maple woods across the eastern US and southern Canada.
animal.season: One generation in the north (May–Aug); two or three in the south (Apr–Sep)

funFact: A pale form in Missouri and Kansas, sometimes called var. alba, is almost entirely white with little or no pink.

summary: One of the heaviest insects on Earth, a flower chafer of the African rainforest whose larvae can weigh around 100 g. Adults are boldly patterned in black and white and fly noisily through the canopy in search of sap and fruit.
nativeRange: Tropical forests of West and Central Africa, from Nigeria and Cameroon to the Congo basin and Uganda
abilities: Larvae can reach about 100 g, among the heaviest insect larvae known
Adult males reach about 11 cm long
Strong fliers despite their bulk, with wings folded under hard wing cases
Larvae need a high-protein diet, unusual among beetle grubs

animal.diet: Adults feed on tree sap and ripe fruit; larvae feed on decaying plant matter in the soil
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest canopy and forest edges
animal.behaviour: Males use a Y-shaped horn on the head to wrestle rivals off feeding sites on tree trunks.
fieldMarks: Very large, broad, flattened scarab
Pronotum white or cream with bold black stripes
Velvety wing cases, black-brown to chestnut with variable white markings
Males with a short forked (Y-shaped) horn; females hornless with a wedge-shaped head for digging
animal.lookalikes: Other Goliathus species differ in pattern: G. regius has mostly white wing cases netted with black; G. orientalis and G. cacicus have their own patterns and ranges. Location and wing-case pattern separate them.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests of Cameroon, Gabon and the Congo basin; captive-bred adults are shown in insect zoos.

lore: Linnaeus described it in 1771 as Scarabaeus goliatus, after the biblical giant Goliath; such beetles were prized centrepieces in European cabinets of curiosities.
funFact: Captive breeders often raise Goliath grubs on dog or cat food mixed into their substrate, because the larvae need far more protein than other scarab larvae.

summary: The longest of all beetles: horned males can reach about 17 cm, more than half of it horn. It ranges from southern Mexico to Bolivia and the Lesser Antilles; some recent studies split the mainland forms into separate species, leaving D. hercules in the strict sense on the Lesser Antilles.
nativeRange: Lesser Antilles (notably Guadeloupe and Dominica) in the strict sense; the wider Dynastes hercules complex ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to the Andes and Amazonia
abilities: Longest beetle in the world, males up to about 17 cm including the horn
Wing cases change from olive-yellow to black as humidity rises, through changes in a porous layer in the cuticle
Males use their pincer-like horns to lift and throw rivals

animal.diet: Adults eat rotting fruit; larvae feed on decaying wood
animal.habitat: Moist rainforest, where larvae develop inside rotting logs
animal.lifespan: Larval stage up to about 2 years; adults about 3–6 months in captivity
animal.size: Males about 5–17 cm including horn; females about 5–8 cm
animal.behaviour: Rival males lock horns, lift one another and slam the loser down or off the branch.
fieldMarks: Male: very long, forward-curving thoracic horn with a brush of golden hairs underneath, opposed by a shorter upcurved head horn
Wing cases olive-green to yellowish with scattered black spots (black when humid)
Head, thorax and horns glossy black
Females hornless, dark and often hairy
animal.lookalikes: Mainland Hercules beetles (D. h. lichyi, septentrionalis, occidentalis and others), treated by some authors as separate species, differ subtly in horn and colour and by range. Neptune beetle (D. neptunus) is all black with extra short horns. Elephant beetles (Megasoma) lack the long thoracic horn.
animal.whereToSee: Montane rainforest of Guadeloupe and Dominica; widely exhibited in insect zoos.

lore: Linnaeus named it Scarabaeus hercules in 1758 after the Greek hero. In Japan, rearing Hercules beetles bought from breeders is a popular hobby.
funFact: The yellow colour comes from a spongy layer in the wing case; when it soaks up water it turns transparent and the black layer beneath shows through.

summary: Europe's largest beetle, whose males carry huge antler-like jaws used only for wrestling rivals. It spends most of its life as a grub in rotting wood underground and emerges for just a few summer weeks.
nativeRange: Europe from southern Sweden to Iberia, east to Turkey, the Caucasus and Syria
abilities: Larvae live 3–6 years feeding on decaying wood
Males' enlarged mandibles function like antlers in contests over females
Adults fly on warm summer evenings with a loud, whirring, upright flight

animal.diet: Larvae eat decaying wood of oak and other broadleaves (stumps, roots); adults sip sap and fruit juice
animal.habitat: Old oak woods, parks, hedgerows and suburban gardens with dead wood
animal.lifespan: Up to about 6 years, almost all as a larva; adults a few weeks
animal.size: Males about 3.5–9 cm including mandibles; females 3–5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males grapple on branches and tree trunks, trying to grip and throw opponents off.
fieldMarks: Male with huge, branched, reddish-brown 'antler' mandibles
Chestnut-brown wing cases and black head and thorax
Female smaller with short, strong jaws
Slow, upright, buzzing flight at dusk
animal.lookalikes: Lesser stag beetle (Dorcus parallelipipedus) is smaller (2–3 cm), all dull black, and has small jaws; female stag beetles have reddish-brown wing cases. Rhinoceros beetle (Sinodendron cylindricum) is small, black and cylindrical.
animal.whereToSee: South-east England (south London, Thames valley, Essex, Kent), and oak woodland across central and southern Europe.
animal.season: Adults late May–July, flying on warm evenings

lore: Pliny the Elder reported that children wore stag-beetle jaws as amulets against illness, and Albrecht Dürer painted a lifelike stag beetle in 1505. Old English folklore blamed it for carrying hot coals and setting thatch alight.
funFact: Despite their size, the male's jaws are too weak to give a painful nip; the smaller-jawed female bites much harder.

summary: A small ground beetle that defends itself with a boiling chemical explosion. Two harmless liquids stored in its abdomen are mixed with enzymes in a reaction chamber, firing a hot, caustic spray with an audible pop.
nativeRange: Europe, especially the south and west, east into western Asia
abilities: Mixes hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide with catalase and peroxidase enzymes to produce a spray near 100 °C
Fires the spray in rapid pulses with an audible crack
Can aim the spray by swivelling the tip of its abdomen

animal.diet: Adults are predators and scavengers of small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Warm, dry, sparsely vegetated ground, often on chalk and limestone; shelters under stones
animal.behaviour: When grabbed by an ant, spider or frog, it blasts the attacker with hot benzoquinones.
fieldMarks: Orange-red head, thorax and legs
Dark metallic blue to blue-green wing cases
Small, narrow ground-beetle shape
Often in groups under stones in dry grassland
animal.lookalikes: Brachinus explodens is smaller (5–7.5 mm) and very similar; a hand lens and key are needed. Other red-and-blue ground beetles (e.g. Lebia, Drypta) lack the defensive pop.
animal.whereToSee: Chalk downland and dry coastal grassland in southern England and continental Europe.
animal.season: Adults mainly Apr–Sep

lore: Linnaeus named it crepitans, 'crackling', in 1758 for its explosive defence. In the late 20th century it became a famous example in debates between creationists and evolutionary biologists over how complex traits evolve.
funFact: High-speed X-ray imaging of bombardier beetles in 2015 showed that each spray is a rapid series of pulses, with an inlet valve to the reaction chamber closing at each blast.

summary: A brilliant metallic-green jewel beetle with rainbow stripes, whose colour comes from structure rather than pigment and never fades. Its wing cases decorate a 7th-century Buddhist shrine in Japan.
nativeRange: Japan, Korea, Taiwan and parts of eastern China
abilities: Iridescent colour produced by microscopic layers in the cuticle, so it lasts for centuries
Larvae bore into dead and dying wood
Adults fly in bright sunshine around the tops of tall trees

animal.diet: Adults eat leaves of Zelkova, hackberry (Celtis) and cherry; larvae feed in the dead wood of these and other broadleaves
animal.habitat: Broadleaf woods, shrine and temple groves, and parks with old trees
animal.behaviour: On hot summer days adults circle the crowns of tall zelkova and hackberry trees, flashing green in the sun.
fieldMarks: Elongated, bullet-shaped beetle
Brilliant metallic green body
Two purple-red stripes running the length of the wing cases and thorax
Flight high around tree crowns in sunshine
animal.lookalikes: Other Chrysochroa jewel beetles of Southeast Asia and the Ryukyus (e.g. C. alternans) differ in the colour and pattern of their stripes and in range.
animal.whereToSee: Temple and shrine groves and parks in Japan with old zelkova and hackberry trees.
animal.season: Adults June–August, peaking in late July

lore: The Tamamushi Shrine at Hōryū-ji, Nara, made in the 7th century, was originally decorated with thousands of these beetles' wing cases set under its metal openwork. Wings of jewel beetles also adorned horse harness from 5th-century Silla tombs in Korea.
funFact: Because the colour is made by stacked nanoscale layers rather than pigment, the beetle wings on the 1,300-year-old Tamamushi Shrine can still shimmer where they survive.

summary: A large predatory water beetle that carries its air supply in a bubble beneath its wing cases. Adults and their fearsome larvae, 'water tigers', hunt tadpoles, newts and even small fish.
nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia
abilities: Stores air under the wing cases and refills by poking its abdomen tip through the surface
Larvae inject digestive enzymes through hollow, sickle-shaped jaws and suck out the liquefied prey
Adults fly at night between ponds and can mistake shiny car roofs and glasshouses for water
Remains active under winter ice

animal.diet: Tadpoles, insect larvae, snails, newts, small fish and carrion
animal.habitat: Well-vegetated ponds, lakes, ditches and slow rivers
animal.behaviour: It swims with both hind legs stroking together like oars, unlike scavenger water beetles which move them alternately.
fieldMarks: Smooth, oval, dark olive-black body
Yellow border around the thorax and wing cases
Males have glossy wing cases and suction pads on the front feet; females usually have grooved wing cases
Fringed, flattened hind legs used as oars
animal.lookalikes: Great silver water beetle (Hydrophilus piceus) is larger, all black, has short clubbed antennae and moves its legs alternately. Other Dytiscus species are separated by the shape of the yellow border and underside colour.
animal.whereToSee: Garden ponds and vegetated lakes across Europe; often netted in pond-dipping sessions.
animal.season: Active year-round; most often seen spring to late summer

funFact: The male's front feet bear sucker discs that help him grip the female during mating; the ridges on many females' wing cases are thought to make that grip harder.

summary: The original 'praying mantis', an ambush predator that waits with spiked forelegs folded as if in prayer. It hears with a single ear in the middle of its chest, tuned to the ultrasound of hunting bats.
nativeRange: Southern and central Europe, Africa and Asia; introduced to North America in the 1890s
abilities: Strikes prey with spiked raptorial forelegs in a fraction of a second
Single midline ear detects bat ultrasound, triggering evasive dives in flight
Turns its head almost 180° to watch prey
Females sometimes eat males during or after mating

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, flies, butterflies, crickets and other insects
animal.habitat: Sunny, tall grassland, scrub, vineyards and gardens
animal.lifespan: About one year: nymphs hatch in spring and adults die in autumn
animal.behaviour: Females lay eggs in a frothy case (ootheca) on stems or stones that hardens and protects up to a few hundred eggs through winter.
fieldMarks: Green or brown, slender body with long neck-like thorax
Raptorial forelegs held folded in front
Black spot ringed with white (a dark 'eye') on the inner base of each foreleg
Wings reach the tip of the abdomen in both sexes
animal.lookalikes: Chinese mantis (Tenodera sinensis), also introduced in North America, is larger (to about 10 cm), lacks the black foreleg spot and has a green-edged wing. Carolina mantis (Stagmomantis carolina) is smaller and the female's wings stop short of the abdomen tip.
animal.whereToSee: Rough grassland and vineyards in southern Europe; meadows and old fields in north-eastern North America.
animal.season: Adults Aug–Oct

lore: The Greek mantis means 'prophet' or 'seer', and in Provence it is called prega-Diéu, 'pray to God'. The entomologist Jean-Henri Fabre made it famous in his Souvenirs entomologiques (1879–1907).
funFact: Its 'cyclopean ear' was discovered in 1986: a single slit between the legs on the underside of the thorax, which makes the mantis deaf to the direction of sound but very sensitive to bat calls.

summary: A flattened, bright-green stick-insect relative that is almost indistinguishable from a leaf, complete with 'veins' and brown 'bite marks'. It even sways gently as if moved by a breeze.
nativeRange: Philippines
abilities: Body and legs are flattened into leaf-like lobes with vein patterns
Rocks from side to side while walking, imitating a leaf in wind
Females can reproduce without males (parthenogenesis)
Eggs look like plant seeds

animal.diet: Leaves of tropical trees and shrubs; in captivity bramble, oak and guava
animal.habitat: Leafy forest canopy and understorey
animal.lifespan: Adults several months; about a year in total
animal.size: Females about 8–9 cm; males smaller (about 5–6 cm) and slimmer
animal.behaviour: Females are flightless and rely on stillness and disguise; slimmer males have full wings and fly to find females.
fieldMarks: Broad, flat, leaf-shaped green body, sometimes with brown or yellow patches
Leaf-like flaps on the legs
Female forewings marked with a pattern resembling a leaf's midrib and veins
Males narrower, with long antennae and functional hindwings
animal.lookalikes: Many Phyllium species are near-identical and are separated by egg shape, the leg lobes and range. In the wild its main 'lookalike' is a leaf.
animal.whereToSee: Philippine forests; one of the most commonly kept leaf insects in captivity.

lore: Leaf insects astonished early European naturalists; Linnaeus named the first known species Gryllus siccifolius, the 'dry-leaf cricket', in 1758.
funFact: Newly hatched nymphs are reddish-brown and look like ants or dead leaf fragments; they turn green only after their first meals of leaves.

summary: A giant cricket-like insect from New Zealand and one of the heaviest insects in the world; a pregnant female has been weighed at 71 g. Wiped out on the mainland by introduced rats, it survived on Hauturu-o-Toi (Little Barrier Island).
nativeRange: Formerly Northland and Auckland region, New Zealand; natural population now only on Hauturu-o-Toi / Little Barrier Island, with translocated populations on other predator-free islands
abilities: One of the heaviest insects ever weighed, up to about 70 g
Wingless and slow, it evolved in the absence of land mammals
Kicks spiny hind legs upward in defence

animal.diet: Leaves of native trees and shrubs; also fruit and flowers
animal.habitat: Forest canopy and scrub; hides by day in tree holes and among foliage
animal.size: Body up to about 10 cm; weight to about 70 g in gravid females
animal.behaviour: It is nocturnal and arboreal, climbing down to the ground mainly to lay eggs in soil.
fieldMarks: Very large, heavy, wingless body, brown with darker bands
Long, thick hind legs covered in spines
Long antennae, longer than the body
Females with a long, curved ovipositor
animal.lookalikes: Tree wētā (Hemideina) are much smaller, and males have very large heads and jaws. Other giant wētā (Deinacrida spp.) occupy different regions of New Zealand.
animal.whereToSee: Hauturu-o-Toi has restricted access; captive-bred wētāpunga are bred at Auckland Zoo and released to islands such as Motuora and Tiritiri Matangi.
animal.season: Year-round; nocturnal

lore: In Māori tradition wētāpunga are named for Punga, ancestor of ugly and deformed creatures. The species' decline began after kiore (Pacific rats) and later European rats reached New Zealand.
funFact: The 71 g record female, weighed in 2011, was photographed eating a carrot from the hand of the naturalist who found her.

summary: A red-eyed cicada that spends 17 years underground feeding on tree roots, then emerges in synchronised billions over a few weeks. Each regional 'brood' appears on its own fixed calendar.
nativeRange: Eastern United States, from the Great Plains to the Atlantic and from the Great Lakes to the Gulf states
abilities: Nymphs count years underground and emerge together after 17 years
Emergence is triggered when soil about 20 cm down reaches roughly 18 °C
Sheer numbers, up to around 1.5 million per acre, overwhelm predators (predator satiation)
Males sing in huge choruses that can exceed 90 decibels

animal.diet: Nymphs drink xylem sap from tree roots; adults feed little, piercing twigs for sap
animal.habitat: Deciduous woods and leafy suburbs
animal.lifespan: 17 years, almost all underground; adults 3–6 weeks
animal.behaviour: Females slit thin twigs to lay eggs, which causes 'flagging' of branch tips; hatchlings drop to the ground and burrow.
fieldMarks: Black body with bright red eyes
Orange wing veins and orange legs
Broad orange bands on the underside of the abdomen
An orange patch behind the eye, above the wing base
animal.voice: Males give a low, buzzing, slightly falling 'phaaa-raoh' call lasting a second or two, repeated and blended into a roaring chorus.
animal.lookalikes: Magicicada cassini is smaller with an all-black abdomen underside and a rapid ticking-then-buzz song; M. septendecula has narrow orange abdominal stripes. The 13-year M. tredecim is very similar but has a lower-pitched song, and the 13-year M. neotredecim can be told apart only by its cycle. Annual dog-day cicadas (Neotibicen) are green and brown with dark eyes.
animal.whereToSee: Leafy suburbs and woods within an emerging brood's range (e.g. Brood X in the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, last seen 2021).
animal.season: Mid-May to late June in emergence years only

edibilityNote: Eaten fried or roasted, as several Indigenous nations and modern foragers have done. People with shellfish allergy may react, as cicadas share allergenic proteins with crustaceans.
lore: William Bradford recorded an emergence at Plymouth Colony in 1633, and colonists called them 'locusts', a misnomer that stuck. Pehr Kalm described the 1749 emergence in Pennsylvania for Linnaeus.
funFact: Brood XIII (17-year) and Brood XIX (13-year) emerged together in 2024 for the first time since 1803; they will not coincide again until 2245.

summary: The cricket of the hearth, a pale-brown chirper that has lived alongside people for thousands of years. Today it is the world's most widely farmed cricket, raised as pet food and increasingly as human food.
nativeRange: Probably south-western Asia; now worldwide in buildings and farms
abilities: Males chirp by rubbing a scraper on one forewing against a file on the other
Hears through ears on its front legs
Completes its life cycle in about two months in warm conditions
Converts feed into protein more efficiently than cattle

animal.diet: Omnivorous: plant matter, grain, scraps and dead insects
animal.habitat: Warm buildings, bakeries, rubbish tips and cricket farms
animal.behaviour: Males call at night to attract females and switch to a softer courtship song once a female is close.
fieldMarks: Light yellowish-brown body
Three dark bands across the top of the head
Long antennae and two long cerci at the tail; females with a long needle-like ovipositor
Wings cover the abdomen
animal.voice: A clear, repeated chirp, 'cree-cree', from males at night; softer ticking courtship song at close range.
animal.lookalikes: Field crickets (Gryllus) are larger and black or dark brown. Tropical house cricket (Gryllodes sigillatus) is smaller with short wings and a banded abdomen.
animal.whereToSee: Pet shops and cricket farms; occasionally in warm buildings and tips.
animal.season: Year-round indoors; outdoors in warm months

edibleParts: whole insect (roasted, fried or ground into powder)
edibilityNote: Sold as whole roasted crickets and cricket flour; approved as a novel food in the EU in 2022. People allergic to shellfish or dust mites may react.
lore: A cricket chirping on the hearth was long thought to bring luck in English homes, the idea behind Charles Dickens's novella The Cricket on the Hearth (1845).
funFact: Crickets' chirp rate rises with temperature, so a calling house cricket is a rough living thermometer.

otherNames: Marabunta (Latin American Spanish, army ants generally)
summary: A nomadic ant whose colonies of hundreds of thousands sweep the rainforest floor in a raiding front many metres wide, flushing out insects as they go. It builds no nest, but sleeps in a living ball of its own workers.
nativeRange: Neotropics, from southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Swarm raids up to about 15 m wide, carrying off huge numbers of insects and other arthropods
Workers link legs to form a living nest (bivouac), bridges and road plugs
Colony alternates between a nomadic phase (moving every night) and a stationary phase while the queen lays eggs
Supports more than 300 associated species, including antbirds that follow its raids

animal.diet: Mostly other arthropods, especially social insects' brood, plus spiders, cockroaches and occasionally small vertebrates
animal.habitat: Lowland rainforest floor and understorey
animal.lifespan: Colonies can persist for years; queens are replaced by budding
animal.size: Workers from about 3 mm to 12 mm; soldiers largest
animal.behaviour: Raids flush fleeing insects that antbirds, woodcreepers and parasitic flies exploit; the bivouac's temperature is regulated by the living ants.
fieldMarks: Dense, broad carpet of reddish-brown to black ants moving across the forest floor
Soldiers with long, pale hook-shaped mandibles
Antbirds calling and flies hovering above the raid front
Columns carrying insect brood back to the bivouac
animal.lookalikes: Eciton hamatum raids in branching columns rather than a broad swarm and preys mostly on other social insects. Labidus army ants raid partly underground and are smaller and darker.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforest reserves such as Barro Colorado Island (Panama), La Selva (Costa Rica) and Amazonian lodges in Peru and Ecuador.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Henry Walter Bates described Eciton army ants in The Naturalist on the River Amazons (1863); the 20th-century studies of T. C. Schneirla on Barro Colorado revealed their nomadic cycle.
funFact: Some antbird species are 'professional' ant-followers that feed almost only at Eciton burchellii raids and check bivouacs each morning to see where the ants will go.

summary: The world's largest hornet, with queens up to about 5 cm long and a 6 mm sting. A few dozen workers can wipe out a European honeybee colony in hours, but Japanese honeybees fight back by cooking scouts alive in a ball of vibrating bodies.
nativeRange: East Asia: Japan, Korea, eastern and central China, Taiwan and the Russian Far East; briefly established in British Columbia and Washington State (2019–2021), declared eradicated from the US in 2024
abilities: Largest hornet in the world
Workers mark a beehive with pheromone and attack in groups, decapitating thousands of bees
Venom contains a neurotoxin (mandaratoxin) and compounds that damage tissue; multiple stings can be fatal
Can fly long distances, foraging several kilometres from the nest

animal.diet: Adults drink tree sap and feed larvae with chewed insects, especially bees and other wasps; larvae give adults a nutritious liquid in return
animal.habitat: Low mountains and forest edges; nests underground in old rodent burrows or rotting root cavities
animal.lifespan: Workers a few weeks to months; colonies last one season, with only mated queens overwintering
animal.size: Queens up to about 5 cm; workers about 3.5–4 cm; wingspan around 7 cm
animal.behaviour: In late summer and autumn, workers enter a 'slaughter phase', killing a hive's adult bees and carrying off the brood to feed their own larvae.
fieldMarks: Very large size
Broad, bright orange-yellow head with large jaws
Dark brown thorax
Abdomen banded dark brown and yellow-orange
animal.lookalikes: European hornet (Vespa crabro) is smaller, with a reddish-brown head and a mostly yellow abdomen. Yellow-legged hornet (V. velutina) is dark with yellow legs. Southern giant hornet (V. soror) of southern China and Southeast Asia is very similar but darker. In North America, cicada killer wasps (Sphecius) and European hornets are commonly mistaken for it.
animal.whereToSee: Forested hills and countryside in Japan and Korea; best viewed in museums or from a safe distance.
animal.season: Queens fly in spring; workers abundant Jul–Oct

lore: In Japan, hornet larvae are eaten in some mountain regions, and a sports drink (VAAM) launched in the 1990s was based on amino acids identified in the liquid larvae feed to adult hornets.
funFact: Japanese honeybees engulf a hornet scout in a ball of hundreds of bees and shiver their flight muscles, raising the temperature to about 46 °C, which kills the hornet but not the bees.

summary: A large rainforest ant whose sting is rated the most painful of any insect, a throbbing pain said to last up to a day. The Sateré-Mawé people of Brazil use it in a coming-of-age ritual.
nativeRange: Lowland rainforests from Honduras and Nicaragua through Central America to the Amazon basin
abilities: Sting rated at the top (4+) of Justin Schmidt's sting pain index
Venom contains poneratoxin, a peptide that keeps nerve sodium channels open
Squeaks (stridulates) and releases a musky odour when disturbed
Workers forage alone up into the canopy

animal.diet: Nectar and other insects, which workers carry back from the canopy
animal.habitat: Nests at the base of rainforest trees; forages on trunks and in the canopy
animal.behaviour: Colonies of a few hundred to a few thousand ants nest among the roots of a single tree and send solitary foragers into its crown.
fieldMarks: Very large reddish-black ant
Large head with strong jaws
Club-shaped tip to the antennae (clavata, 'club-bearing')
Single node between thorax and abdomen with a visible sting
animal.lookalikes: Giant Amazonian ants (Dinoponera) are larger, all black and lack clubbed antennae. Ectatomma and Neoponera species are smaller.
animal.whereToSee: Tree bases along rainforest trails in Costa Rica (La Selva), Panama and Amazonian Peru and Ecuador.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: In the Sateré-Mawé initiation, young men wear woven gloves filled with sedated bullet ants, stingers pointing inward, for several minutes at a time, repeating the ordeal many times over months.
funFact: The Spanish name 'veinticuatro' (twenty-four) refers to the claim that the pain of one sting lasts 24 hours.

summary: A small mosquito that is one of the deadliest animals on Earth because its females transmit the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Malaria still kills around 600,000 people a year, most of them children in sub-Saharan Africa.
nativeRange: Sub-Saharan Africa
abilities: Females strongly prefer human blood and bite mainly at night, often indoors
Larvae develop in small, sunlit, temporary pools such as puddles and hoofprints, in about a week
Transmits Plasmodium falciparum, the most lethal malaria parasite
Some populations have evolved resistance to the insecticides on bed nets

animal.diet: Females take blood (mainly human) to develop eggs; both sexes drink nectar and plant juices
animal.habitat: Near people in rural and peri-urban Africa; larvae in shallow, sunny standing water
animal.behaviour: Males gather in dusk swarms over landmarks, and females fly into the swarm to mate once.
fieldMarks: Rests with body angled steeply to the surface, proboscis and body in a straight line
Wings spotted with pale and dark scales
Female palps as long as the proboscis
Larvae lie flat beneath the water surface (no breathing siphon)
animal.lookalikes: Anopheles coluzzii and A. arabiensis are sibling species that look identical and are told apart only by DNA. Culex mosquitoes rest with the body parallel to the surface and have unspotted wings.
animal.whereToSee: Villages and farmland across tropical Africa, especially in the rainy season.
animal.season: Peaks in the rainy season when temporary pools form

lore: Ronald Ross showed in 1897 that Anopheles mosquitoes carry malaria, winning a Nobel Prize in 1902. A member of the A. gambiae complex that invaded north-eastern Brazil in 1930 was eradicated by a campaign led by Fred Soper by 1940.
funFact: In 2018 a gene drive targeting the doublesex gene crashed caged populations of A. gambiae to zero within 7–11 generations.

summary: Probably the most widespread insect in human company, breeding in dung and rotting waste wherever people live. It tastes with its feet, eats by spitting digestive juices onto food, and can carry the germs of typhoid, cholera and dysentery on its body.
nativeRange: Probably originated in the Middle East or Central Asia; now worldwide wherever people live
abilities: Completes egg-to-adult development in about a week in warm weather
Tastes food with sensory hairs on its feet
Females lay roughly 500 eggs in batches over their lives
Mechanically spreads disease-causing bacteria, viruses and parasites
Larvae can convert manure and food waste into protein-rich biomass

animal.diet: Adults liquefy food with saliva and sponge it up: sugars, rotting matter, dung, food scraps; larvae feed in manure and decaying waste
animal.habitat: Homes, farms, markets and anywhere with garbage or manure
animal.behaviour: It cannot bite or chew; instead it regurgitates digestive fluid onto food and laps it up with a sponge-like mouth.
fieldMarks: Grey thorax with four dark lengthwise stripes
Large reddish-brown eyes (closer together in males)
Abdomen grey to yellowish with a dark midline
A sharp upward bend in the fourth long wing vein
animal.lookalikes: Lesser house fly (Fannia canicularis) is smaller and flies in slow circles under lights. Stable fly (Stomoxys calcitrans) has a forward-pointing piercing proboscis and bites. Flesh flies (Sarcophagidae) are larger with three thorax stripes and a chequered abdomen.
animal.whereToSee: Practically anywhere people live, especially near livestock and waste.
animal.season: Year-round in warm places; summer peak in temperate regions

lore: The Philistine god Baal-zebub, 'Lord of the Flies' in 2 Kings, became the Beelzebub of later Jewish and Christian tradition; William Golding borrowed the phrase for his 1954 novel.
funFact: Its maggots are now farmed in some countries to turn manure and food waste into protein feed for poultry and fish.

summary: The heaviest spider in the world, a tarantula of northern South American rainforests that can weigh over 150 g with a leg span near 30 cm. Despite its name it seldom eats birds, feeding mostly on earthworms, insects and frogs.
nativeRange: Northern South America: Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and northern Brazil
abilities: Heaviest spider known, recorded at over 170 g
Flicks clouds of barbed, irritating hairs from its abdomen at attackers
Makes a loud hissing sound by rubbing bristles on its legs
Fangs about 2–4 cm long

animal.diet: Earthworms, large insects, frogs, lizards and small rodents; birds only rarely
animal.habitat: Deep burrows in moist soil of swampy or upland rainforest
animal.lifespan: Females 15–25 years; males only a few years
animal.size: Leg span up to about 28–30 cm; body up to about 12 cm
animal.behaviour: It sits at its burrow entrance at night and ambushes passing prey, detecting vibrations through silk threads laid around the opening.
fieldMarks: Enormous, heavy-bodied, hairy brown tarantula
Uniform brown with faint pale rings on the legs
Large, rounded abdomen with a bald patch where irritating hairs have been flicked
Mature males lack the tibial hooks found in similar Theraphosa
animal.lookalikes: Pinkfoot goliath (Theraphosa apophysis) has pinkish feet and males with tibial hooks. Burgundy goliath (T. stirmi) is darker with reddish hairs. Giant huntsman (Heteropoda maxima) of Laos has a wider leg span but is flat and lightweight.
animal.whereToSee: Rainforests of Guyana, Suriname and southern Venezuela; often kept in zoos and by tarantula hobbyists.
animal.season: Year-round; nocturnal

edibilityNote: Eaten roasted by Indigenous peoples of Venezuela and Guyana, who first singe off the irritating hairs; the hairs can injure eyes and skin.
lore: The name 'bird-eater' traces back to Maria Sibylla Merian's 1705 Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium, which showed a large tarantula eating a hummingbird in Suriname.
funFact: Its venom is weak to humans, roughly comparable to a wasp sting; the hairs it flicks are usually the bigger nuisance.

summary: A glossy black spider with a red hourglass on its belly, carrying one of the most potent spider venoms in North America. Its neurotoxin, α-latrotoxin, causes intense muscle pain and cramps, although deaths are now very rare.
nativeRange: South-eastern United States, from Florida north to about New York and west to Texas and Oklahoma
abilities: Venom contains α-latrotoxin, which makes nerve endings release neurotransmitter in a flood
Builds strong, irregular cobwebs with sticky gumfoot lines that snare walking prey
Silk is exceptionally strong and fine

animal.diet: Insects and other arthropods such as beetles, crickets and other spiders
animal.habitat: Dark, sheltered spots: woodpiles, rock walls, sheds, outhouses and under ledges
animal.lifespan: Females 1–3 years; males a few months
animal.size: Female body about 8–13 mm; male much smaller
animal.behaviour: Females hang upside down in their webs and display the red hourglass; cannibalism of males after mating happens but is less common in the wild than its reputation suggests.
fieldMarks: Female shiny jet-black with a round abdomen
Complete red hourglass on the underside of the abdomen
Often a red spot just above the spinnerets on the back
Messy, tangled web near the ground
animal.lookalikes: Northern black widow (Latrodectus variolus) has its hourglass split into two separate marks and a row of red spots on the back. Western black widow (L. hesperus) lives further west. False widows (Steatoda) are brownish and lack the red hourglass.
animal.whereToSee: Woodpiles, stone walls and outbuildings in the south-eastern US; look with a torch at night, but never touch or handle.
animal.season: Year-round in the south; most noticed late summer and autumn

lore: The genus name Latrodectus means roughly 'robber-biter' and mactans 'murderous'. During the Second World War, black widow silk was used for the crosshairs of gun and bomb sights.
funFact: Bites cause latrodectism: severe cramping abdominal pain that has been mistaken for appendicitis; an antivenom exists for serious cases.

summary: A jumping spider about 5 mm long whose males raise a brilliantly coloured flap on the abdomen like a peacock's fan and dance for females. If the female is not impressed she may eat him.
nativeRange: Eastern Australia, mainly coastal New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland
abilities: Males unfold and raise iridescent abdominal flaps during courtship
Combines visual display with vibrations drummed through the ground
Excellent vision, including colour vision, typical of jumping spiders

animal.diet: Small insects and other arthropods, stalked and pounced on
animal.habitat: Leaf litter and low vegetation in heath, scrub and woodland
animal.behaviour: The male lifts his third pair of legs, raises his patterned flap, and sidesteps and shimmies in front of the female.
fieldMarks: Tiny jumping spider with large front eyes
Male abdomen patterned in red, orange, blue and green, with fold-out side flaps
Male third legs black with white tips, raised in display
Females mottled brown and grey
animal.lookalikes: Dozens of other Maratus species, most described since 2010, differ in the pattern and colours of the male's fan; females are very hard to tell apart.
animal.whereToSee: Heath and bushland around Sydney (e.g. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park) and in south-east Queensland.
animal.season: Mature males Aug–Dec, displaying in the austral spring

lore: Octavius Pickard-Cambridge described it in 1874 and named it volans, 'flying', after a collector's report that the flaps helped it glide. The photographs and films of Jürgen Otto made peacock spiders internet-famous from the 2010s.
funFact: Its flaps cannot be used for gliding at all; they are purely for courtship.

summary: A large orb-weaving spider striped like a wasp in yellow, black and white, that decorates its web with a bold zig-zag band of silk. It has spread rapidly northward across Europe in recent decades.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia to Japan; expanding northward
abilities: Builds a zig-zag silk band (stabilimentum) whose function is debated, possibly deterring birds or attracting prey
Spiderlings disperse by 'ballooning' on silk threads carried by the wind
Males often mate with females just after their final moult, when females are least dangerous

animal.diet: Grasshoppers, crickets, flies, bees and other flying or jumping insects
animal.habitat: Tall grass in sunny meadows, heath, dunes and verges
animal.size: Females about 1.4–1.7 cm body length (up to about 2.5 cm); males about 0.5 cm
animal.behaviour: Males are frequently cannibalised by females during mating, and often leave part of their palp in the female as a mating plug.
fieldMarks: Female abdomen striped yellow, black and white like a wasp
Silvery-haired cephalothorax
Banded legs held in an X shape at the hub of the web
Orb web low in grass with a vertical zig-zag silk band
animal.lookalikes: Lobed argiope (Argiope lobata) of southern Europe has a silvery, scalloped abdomen. The North American banded garden spider (A. trifasciata) has thinner stripes. Garden spiders (Araneus) lack the bold stripes.
animal.whereToSee: Rough grassland and coastal meadows across Europe; now common in southern England.
animal.season: Adults Jul–Oct

lore: Giovanni Scopoli named it in 1772 after the Danish zoologist Morten Thrane Brünnich. Its arrival in Britain was first noted in the early 20th century, and its range expansion is now followed as a sign of climate change.
funFact: Its egg sac is a brown, paper-like urn hung among grass stems, in which the young overwinter before emerging in spring.

summary: A slender straw-yellow scorpion of north-east African deserts whose venom is among the most dangerous of any scorpion. The same venom has yielded chlorotoxin, a molecule now used to make brain tumours glow during surgery.
nativeRange: North-eastern Africa, chiefly Egypt and Sudan into the Horn of Africa; related Leiurus species formerly included in it range across Arabia and the Levant
abilities: Venom mixes several neurotoxins that can cause intense pain, convulsions, heart failure and pulmonary oedema
Chlorotoxin from its venom binds selectively to glioma cells and is used in tumour-imaging agents
Glows blue-green under ultraviolet light, like all scorpions
Can survive long periods without food

animal.diet: Insects, spiders, other scorpions and small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Dry, rocky or sandy desert and scrub; shelters under stones and in burrows
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night, relying on venom rather than its slender pincers to subdue prey.
fieldMarks: Straw-yellow to pale yellow-brown body
Slender, weak-looking pincers
Long, thin tail with a darker last segment and sting
Five keels (ridges) along the back, giving the name quinquestriatus, 'five-striped'
animal.lookalikes: Other Leiurus species (e.g. L. hebraeus in the Levant) are separated by fine details and range. Fat-tailed scorpions (Androctonus) have much thicker tails and are often darker. Buthus species are similar but have different ridge patterns.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky desert in Egypt and Sudan, where it glows under ultraviolet light at night; best seen in zoos. Never handle it, and shake out shoes and bedding in its range.
animal.season: Year-round; most active on warm nights

lore: Scorpions were the emblem of Serqet, the ancient Egyptian goddess who healed stings and venomous bites. A peptide toxin from this scorpion's venom, charybdotoxin, became a standard tool for studying potassium channels.
funFact: An imaging drug derived from chlorotoxin, nicknamed 'Tumor Paint', has been tested in clinical trials to help surgeons see the edges of brain tumours.

summary: A reddish-brown scorpion of rural India and Pakistan, often described as the most lethal scorpion in the world. Its venom triggers a storm in the nervous system that damages the heart and lungs, but cheap treatment with the drug prazosin has made deaths far rarer.
nativeRange: India, Pakistan and eastern Nepal
abilities: Venom causes a massive release of adrenaline-like hormones (autonomic storm)
Stings can cause high blood pressure, heart failure and fluid on the lungs
Thrives around village houses, cattle sheds and stone walls

animal.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Rubble, crevices in mud and stone walls, under stones, and inside village houses
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night and often hides in shoes, clothing and bedding, where most human stings happen.
fieldMarks: Reddish- to orange-brown body
Relatively slender pincers
Thick, segmented tail with prominent ridges
Dark-grey keels on the back of the abdomen
animal.lookalikes: Giant forest scorpions (Heterometrus) are larger, shiny black with massive pincers and much weaker venom. Other Hottentotta and Lychas species are smaller or differently patterned.
animal.whereToSee: Rural areas of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh; most stings occur in the hot season and monsoon.
animal.season: Year-round; most encountered in summer and monsoon

lore: The rural Maharashtra physician Himmatrao Bawaskar showed from the 1980s that prazosin, a blood-pressure drug, counteracts the venom; in his patient series, death rates fell from around 30–40% to under 1%.
funFact: Children are at greatest risk, because the same dose of venom is far more concentrated in a small body.

summary: The only spider that lives almost entirely underwater. It spins a silk 'diving bell' among water plants, fills it with air carried down from the surface, and eats, moults, mates and raises young inside.
nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia, east to Japan
abilities: Carries air down on its hairy abdomen, which looks silver underwater
Its bell works as a physical gill: oxygen diffuses in from the water, so it needs to refill only rarely
Males are larger than females, unusual among spiders
Overwinters in a sealed bell or empty snail shell

animal.diet: Aquatic insects, water lice and other small aquatic animals
animal.habitat: Clean, still or slow water with dense submerged plants
animal.behaviour: It waits in its bell with legs touching silk lines, then darts out to seize passing prey and drags it inside to eat.
fieldMarks: Spider moving underwater with a shining silver air bubble around its abdomen
Dull dark-brown, velvety body
Thimble-sized silvery bell of silk among water plants
Long, fine hairs on legs and abdomen
animal.lookalikes: Raft spiders (Dolomedes) are larger, striped, and hunt on the water surface rather than living below it. Pirate wolf spiders (Pirata) dive briefly but live on land.
animal.whereToSee: Clean, plant-rich ponds and fen ditches in Europe, e.g. the Norfolk Broads and Somerset Levels in England.
animal.season: Year-round; most active spring to autumn

lore: Carl Clerck described it in Svenska Spindlar (1757), the work that is the official starting point for scientific names of spiders.
funFact: Measurements in 2011 showed a diving bell spider can stay in its bell for more than a day without surfacing, because oxygen seeps into the bubble from the surrounding water.

summary: The largest octopus in the world, with an arm span that can reach about 4 m. Clever and curious, it lives only 3–5 years, and a female dies after guarding her eggs for half a year without eating.
nativeRange: Temperate North Pacific, from Japan and Korea through the Russian Far East and Aleutians to Alaska, British Columbia and California
abilities: Largest octopus species; adults commonly 10–50 kg
Changes skin colour and texture in a fraction of a second
Captive individuals recognise and respond differently to particular people
Can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak
Each sucker can taste and grip independently

animal.diet: Crabs, clams, scallops, snails, fish and occasionally sharks and seabirds
animal.habitat: Rocky dens from the intertidal zone down to around 2,000 m
animal.size: Typically 10–50 kg with an arm span of up to about 4 m; verified records reach about 70 kg
animal.behaviour: A brooding female hangs strings of up to tens of thousands of eggs from her den roof and cleans and aerates them for about six months before dying soon after they hatch.
fieldMarks: Very large octopus, reddish-brown when relaxed
Wrinkled, folded skin with small flap-like papillae
Paddle-shaped papillae near the eyes
Piles of crab shells and clam shells (a 'midden') outside the den
animal.lookalikes: East Pacific red octopus (Octopus rubescens) is much smaller (rarely over 0.5 kg) with three eyelash-like papillae under each eye. Large size alone usually identifies the giant Pacific.
animal.whereToSee: Cold-water dive sites in Puget Sound and British Columbia (e.g. Browning Pass, Seattle's Seacrest Park); public aquariums.
animal.season: Year-round

edibilityNote: Fished in Japan (Hokkaido), Korea and Alaska and eaten boiled or raw.
lore: It is named after Franz Doflein, a German zoologist who studied the marine life of Japan around 1904–05. In Hokkaido it has long been caught in traditional octopus pots.
funFact: About two-thirds of its nerve cells lie in its arms rather than its brain, so each arm can taste, grip and react partly on its own.

summary: A master of disguise that can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in under a second, despite being colour-blind. Its ink gave artists the pigment sepia, and its internal shell, the cuttlebone, washes up on European beaches.
nativeRange: Eastern Atlantic from the North Sea and Baltic approaches south to north-west Africa; Mediterranean Sea
abilities: Millions of chromatophores give rapid, patterned colour change
Raises skin papillae to mimic rocks and seaweed
Sees polarised light and uses it in signalling
Adjusts buoyancy by pumping fluid in and out of its chambered cuttlebone
Ejects clouds of melanin ink

animal.diet: Shrimps, crabs and small fish, caught with two shooting tentacles
animal.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, seagrass and sandy bottoms, down to about 200 m
animal.size: Mantle up to about 45 cm; weight up to about 4 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring, adults move inshore to spawn; small males have been reported to mimic females to slip past large rival males and mate, a tactic better known in the giant Australian cuttlefish.
fieldMarks: Broad, oval, flattened body with a narrow fin running around the entire edge
W-shaped pupils
Eight short arms plus two long feeding tentacles
Breeding males show bold black-and-white 'zebra' stripes
animal.lookalikes: Elegant cuttlefish (Sepia elegans) and pink cuttlefish (S. orbignyana) are smaller and pinkish, with a sharp spine at the rear of the cuttlebone. Squid have fins only at the tail end, and octopuses have no fins.
animal.whereToSee: Seagrass and sandy bays in the Mediterranean and along the English Channel and Biscay coasts; cuttlebones on beaches in summer.
animal.season: Inshore spawning Apr–Jul

edibilityNote: Eaten grilled, fried and stewed across the Mediterranean; the ink colours black rice and pasta dishes.
lore: Aristotle described its ink, mating and egg-laying in his History of Animals. Brown 'sepia' ink made from it was used for writing and drawing, and the name of the genus became a word for the colour.
funFact: Its cuttlebone is sold as a calcium supplement for caged birds.

summary: A living relative of the ammonites, carrying a coiled, chambered shell striped with flame-like bands. Its lineage has changed little for hundreds of millions of years, but demand for its shells has driven heavy local declines.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-West Pacific: the Philippines, Indonesia, New Guinea, northern and eastern Australia, and Melanesia
abilities: Controls buoyancy by moving fluid and gas through its shell chambers via a tube called the siphuncle
Has about 90 suckerless tentacles
Pinhole-camera eyes with no lens
Lives far longer than most cephalopods, possibly 15–20 years

animal.diet: Scavenges dead fish, crustaceans, moulted crab shells and carrion
animal.habitat: Steep reef slopes from about 100 m to over 500 m, rising shallower at night
animal.size: Shell usually about 15–20 cm across; exceptionally to about 25 cm
animal.behaviour: It moves by jet propulsion, rising up reef walls at night to feed and sinking deeper by day, possibly to avoid predators and warm water.
fieldMarks: Smooth, coiled, cream-white shell with orange-brown tiger stripes fading towards the opening
Closed centre of the coil (no open navel)
Leathery hood over the head
Many slender tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Crusty nautilus (Allonautilus scrobiculatus) has an open navel and a hairy shell covering. Palau nautilus (N. belauensis) and New Caledonian nautilus (N. macromphalus) differ in shell shape and range.
animal.whereToSee: Deep reef walls in Palau, the Philippines and the Coral Sea (Osprey Reef), usually by baited camera; public aquariums.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Georg Rumphius described the nautilus in D'Amboinsche Rariteitkamer (1705). Renaissance goldsmiths mounted the shells as ornate 'nautilus cups' for European cabinets of curiosities.
funFact: Its shell is a logarithmic spiral, but measurements show it does not follow the golden ratio, despite the popular claim.

summary: The largest living clam, reaching over 1.3 m long and 200 kg, that farms algae in its own flesh. Sunlight on its colourful mantle feeds the algae, which in turn feed the clam.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific: Great Barrier Reef, the Philippines, Indonesia, Micronesia and Melanesia; extinct in several former parts of its range
abilities: Hosts symbiotic zooxanthellae algae in its mantle, which supply most of its food
Iridescent cells in the mantle spread and shield light for the algae
One of the longest-lived invertebrates, possibly over 100 years
Filters plankton from seawater

animal.diet: Sugars from symbiotic algae, plus filtered plankton
animal.habitat: Sandy patches and reef flats in clear, shallow water, usually less than 20 m deep
animal.size: Shell up to about 1.4 m; weight over 200 kg
animal.behaviour: Adults sit hinge-down on sand, unattached, and spawn by releasing clouds of eggs and sperm into the water.
fieldMarks: Huge, heavy shell with four to six broad, deep folds
Wavy, interlocking shell margin
Golden-brown to olive mantle with iridescent blue-green spots
Lies free on the bottom; large adults cannot close fully
animal.lookalikes: Smooth giant clam (Tridacna derasa) has a smoother shell with lower ribs. Fluted giant clam (T. squamosa) has rows of scale-like flutes. Small giant clams (T. maxima, T. crocea) are much smaller and bore into coral.
animal.whereToSee: Reefs of the northern Great Barrier Reef (e.g. Lizard Island), Palau, and restocking sites in the Philippines (Bolinao, Pangasinan).
animal.season: Year-round

edibilityNote: The adductor muscle is prized in Asian cuisine; overharvesting for meat and shells caused its collapse. Only farmed animals should be eaten.
lore: Giant clam shells serve as holy-water fonts (bénitiers) in European churches, notably the pair in Saint-Sulpice, Paris, said to be a gift from the Republic of Venice to King Francis I.
funFact: The 'man-eating clam' that traps divers is a myth; adults close too slowly to trap anyone, and there is no reliable record of a death.

summary: A golf-ball-sized octopus that flashes vivid blue rings when alarmed. Its saliva carries tetrodotoxin, a nerve poison that can paralyse and kill an adult human within minutes to hours, and there is no antivenom.
nativeRange: Tropical western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean: northern Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, north to southern Japan
abilities: Saliva carries tetrodotoxin produced by symbiotic bacteria
Flashes about 60 blue rings in a fraction of a second, using muscles that expose reflecting layers
Bite is often painless, so victims may not notice it
Can change from drab brown to warning colours instantly

animal.diet: Small crabs, shrimps and fish, subdued by injecting venomous saliva
animal.habitat: Shallow reefs, rubble, tide pools and seagrass, often hiding in shells and crevices
animal.behaviour: Normally camouflaged in brown and yellow, it displays pulsing blue rings when provoked, a warning to predators.
fieldMarks: Tiny octopus, yellowish-brown at rest
Large, iridescent blue rings outlined in black, larger than in other blue-ringed species
Rings flash brightly when the animal is disturbed
Often found in empty shells or bottles
animal.lookalikes: Southern blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena maculosa) of southern Australia is smaller with smaller rings. Blue-lined octopus (H. fasciata) has blue lines on the body rather than rings. Treat any blue-ringed octopus as deadly.
animal.whereToSee: Muck-diving sites such as Lembeh Strait (Indonesia) and Anilao (Philippines); never handle.
animal.season: Year-round
