lore: Blue-ringed octopus bites killed swimmers in Australia in the 1950s and 1960s, and the animal became a pop-culture emblem in the James Bond film Octopussy (1983).
funFact: Victims stay conscious while paralysed; people have survived when bystanders gave artificial respiration until the toxin wore off.

summary: A beautifully patterned sea snail responsible for most of the recorded human deaths from cone snails. It hunts fish by engulfing them in a net-like mouth after releasing a cocktail of venoms that includes a fast-acting insulin.
nativeRange: Tropical Indo-Pacific, from East Africa and the Red Sea to Japan, Australia and Polynesia
abilities: Fires a harpoon-like hollow tooth loaded with venom
Releases weaponised insulin into the water to send nearby fish into hypoglycaemic shock
Venom contains hundreds of different conotoxin peptides
Can kill a human; dozens of deaths are documented

animal.diet: Small fish, engulfed in an expandable mouth (rostrum)
animal.habitat: Reef flats, lagoons and sandy patches between corals
animal.behaviour: It hunts at night, spreading its false mouth over resting fish, which are sedated by venom and insulin before being stung and swallowed whole.
fieldMarks: Thin, light, broad cone shell with a wide aperture
Shoulder of the spire crowned with low knobs
Whitish to pinkish with brown net-like and blotchy bands, like an old map
Buried in sand by day
animal.lookalikes: Tulip cone (Conus tulipa) is smaller with a violet-pink tinge; textile cone (C. textile) has a tent-shaped triangular pattern. All cone snails should be treated as dangerous.
animal.whereToSee: Indo-Pacific reefs at night; often seen in shell collections. Never pick up a live cone.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: Georg Rumphius recorded in 1705 that a woman on Ambon died after holding a live cone shell; Japanese call it Anboina-gai, the 'Ambon shell'.
funFact: Fish-hunting cones like this one helped researchers discover very fast-acting insulin forms that are being studied for diabetes treatment.

summary: Europe's largest land snail and the classic escargot de Bourgogne. It seals itself in for winter behind a chalky door and can live for 20 years.
nativeRange: Central and south-eastern Europe; introduced in Britain (probably in Roman times), Scandinavia and elsewhere
abilities: Seals its shell in winter with a thick, chalky epiphragm
Shoots a calcium 'love dart' into its partner during courtship
Hermaphrodite: each snail both gives and receives sperm
Can live about 20 years or more

animal.diet: Green plants, fallen leaves and fruit
animal.habitat: Lime-rich soils: chalk and limestone grassland, open woods, hedgerows and vineyards
animal.lifespan: Often 6–10 years in the wild; up to about 20 years or more
animal.size: Shell about 4–5 cm high and wide
animal.behaviour: Before winter it buries itself in soil and seals the shell opening, slowing its heartbeat and breathing until spring.
fieldMarks: Large, globular shell, creamy-buff to light brown
Faint, broad, pale brownish bands
Body pale grey-cream with a coarse, net-like texture
Lip of the shell only slightly thickened
animal.lookalikes: Garden snail (Cornu aspersum) is smaller with a glossy brown shell mottled in darker bands. Turkish snail (Helix lucorum) has bold, dark-brown bands.
animal.whereToSee: Chalk downs of southern England (e.g. North Downs, Chilterns) and limestone country across central Europe after rain.
animal.season: Active Apr–Oct; hibernates in winter

edibilityNote: Eaten as escargots after purging and cooking. Wild snails are protected in Britain and several other countries, so commercial supplies are farmed or imported.
lore: Pliny the Elder credited Fulvius Lippinus with founding the first snail parks near Tarquinia in the 1st century BCE, fattening snails for Roman tables.
funFact: Courtship can last hours, the pair circling and caressing each other before one fires its chalky love dart.

summary: The second-largest slug in the world, a bright yellow giant of the Pacific Northwest rainforest floor. It recycles leaf litter, dung and fungi into soil and spreads seeds and spores as it goes.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from south-eastern Alaska to California
abilities: Grows to about 25 cm long
Thick slime protects from drying out and deters predators
Smells with tentacles and can follow slime trails to find mates
Hermaphrodite; both partners exchange sperm

animal.diet: Leaf litter, fungi, moss, dead plants and animal droppings
animal.habitat: Moist forest floor of conifer and redwood forests
animal.behaviour: It feeds and moves mostly in cool, wet weather, retreating under logs in dry spells, and acts as a decomposer.
fieldMarks: Very large, smooth slug
Yellow to greenish with black spots, or olive to brown
Saddle-like mantle near the head with a breathing hole on the right side
Two pairs of tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Leopard slug (Limax maximus), an introduced European species, is grey with black spots or stripes and a ridge along the tail. Other Ariolimax species occupy different parts of California.
animal.whereToSee: Damp trails in Olympic National Park, coastal British Columbia and the redwood parks of northern California.
animal.season: Year-round in wet weather; most active in the rainy months

lore: Banana slugs are emblems of the Pacific Northwest forests; a related species, Ariolimax dolichophallus, is the mascot of the University of California, Santa Cruz.
funFact: Its eyes sit at the tips of the upper tentacles, which it pulls back into its head when touched.

summary: The largest land-living arthropod, a giant hermit crab that abandons its borrowed shell and can weigh 4 kg with legs spanning about a metre. Its claws pinch with a force rivalling the bite of a lion, enough to crack open coconuts.
nativeRange: Islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, from Zanzibar, Aldabra and the Chagos through Christmas Island and Indonesia to Micronesia and Polynesia
abilities: Pinching force measured at over 3,300 newtons, among the strongest of any crustacean
Opens coconuts by stripping the husk and hammering the shell
Breathes air with modified gills ('branchiostegal lungs') and drowns if kept underwater
Climbs trees and can live 60 years or more

animal.diet: Coconuts, fruit, nuts, carrion, other crabs, and occasionally birds and rats
animal.habitat: Coastal forest and rocky areas on islands, sheltering in burrows and crevices by day
animal.size: Up to about 4 kg and a leg span of about 1 m
animal.behaviour: Females release eggs into the sea at high tide; larvae drift for weeks, then young crabs come ashore using snail shells before outgrowing them.
fieldMarks: Enormous land crab with a hard, curled-under abdomen and no shell
Colour varies from violet-blue to orange-red
Very large front claws, the left usually bigger
Long, sturdy antennae
animal.lookalikes: Land hermit crabs (Coenobita) are much smaller and keep living in snail shells as adults. Juvenile coconut crabs also use shells and are told apart by their heavier claws and colour.
animal.whereToSee: Christmas Island (Indian Ocean), Aldabra, the Chagos atolls, Vanuatu and Niue, mostly at night.
animal.season: Year-round; most active at night

edibleParts: meat of legs, claws and abdomen (cooked)
edibilityNote: Prized as a delicacy on Pacific islands, but heavy harvesting threatens it and many places protect it. Crabs that have eaten toxic plants (such as Cerbera) have occasionally poisoned people.
lore: Charles Darwin described coconut crabs on the Keeling Islands in The Voyage of the Beagle, noting how they tear husks fibre by fibre before breaking the shell.
funFact: In 2016 a coconut crab on the Chagos Islands was observed killing and eating a red-footed booby, confirming it can prey on birds.

summary: The largest crab in the world by leg span, reaching about 3.7 m from claw tip to claw tip. It lives in deep water off Japan's Pacific coast and climbs to shallower depths to breed in spring.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of Japan, especially Sagami Bay, Suruga Bay and Tosa Bay; also reported off Taiwan
abilities: Largest leg span of any arthropod, up to about 3.7 m
Can regenerate lost legs over successive moults
Young crabs camouflage themselves by attaching sponges and other organisms to their shells

animal.diet: Scavenger and opportunist: dead animals, molluscs and other invertebrates, plus algae
animal.habitat: Sandy and rocky bottoms from about 50 to 600 m deep
animal.size: Leg span up to about 3.7 m; carapace up to about 40 cm; weight up to about 19 kg
animal.behaviour: In spring it moves into waters around 50 m deep to mate and spawn, when fishing for it is restricted.
fieldMarks: Enormously long, thin legs
Orange body and legs with white spots
Pear-shaped, bumpy carapace
Long, thin claws in males
animal.lookalikes: King crabs (Paralithodes) are spiny, have shorter legs and appear to have only three pairs of walking legs. Snow crabs (Chionoecetes) have a flat, rounded shell and much shorter legs.
animal.whereToSee: Large public aquariums in Japan (e.g. Osaka Kaiyukan, Numazu Deep Sea Aquarium) and worldwide; divers occasionally see them in Suruga Bay in spring.
animal.season: Moves shallower to breed in spring

edibilityNote: Eaten locally around Suruga Bay (e.g. Heda on the Izu Peninsula); catches have declined and are managed.
lore: It is named after Engelbert Kaempfer, the German physician who worked at the Dutch trading post of Dejima in the 1690s and wrote one of the first European histories of Japan.
funFact: Its long legs are fragile; it often lives with lost or regrowing legs, which it replaces gradually over several moults.

summary: A shrimp-like crustacean only about 6 cm long whose total weight, hundreds of millions of tonnes, may be the largest of any wild animal species. Almost everything in the Southern Ocean depends on it, from penguins to blue whales.
nativeRange: Southern Ocean around Antarctica, densest in the Scotia Sea and Antarctic Peninsula
abilities: Forms swarms with tens of thousands of individuals per cubic metre
Grazes algae from the underside of sea ice in winter
Can shrink by moulting when food is short
Has light-producing organs (photophores)
Moves carbon to the deep sea in its faeces and moults

animal.diet: Phytoplankton, especially diatoms, and ice algae; some small zooplankton
animal.habitat: Cold open ocean and the sea-ice zone of the Southern Ocean
animal.size: Up to about 6 cm and 2 g
animal.behaviour: Swarms rise towards the surface at night and sink by day, possibly to avoid visual predators.
fieldMarks: Transparent to pinkish shrimp-like body
Large, black, light-sensitive eyes
Feathery legs forming a 'feeding basket'
Green-coloured gut when feeding on algae
animal.lookalikes: Ice krill (Euphausia crystallorophias) is smaller and lives closer to the continent. Thysanoessa species are smaller and more slender.
animal.whereToSee: Surface swarms seen from expedition ships around South Georgia and the Antarctic Peninsula, often signalled by feeding whales and seabirds.
animal.season: Year-round; most visible near the surface in the austral summer (Nov–Mar)

edibilityNote: Fished mainly for aquaculture feed and omega-3 krill-oil supplements; also processed into human food in Japan. Fresh krill spoils quickly and has high fluoride in its shell.
lore: The word 'krill' comes from Norwegian whalers, meaning the small fry of fish. Britain's Discovery Investigations of the 1920s–30s first mapped its role in the whaling grounds.
funFact: Estimates of its global biomass are around 300–500 million tonnes, comparable to the total weight of all humans.

summary: The heaviest crustacean in the world, with the record animal weighing about 20 kg. It carries two different claws, a heavy crusher and a sharp cutter, and may live for a century.
nativeRange: North-west Atlantic, from Labrador to North Carolina
abilities: Heaviest crustacean on record (about 20 kg)
Two specialised claws: a blunt crusher and a sharp pincer
Regenerates lost legs and claws
Locates food by smell with its antennules and leg hairs

animal.diet: Crabs, molluscs, sea urchins, worms, fish and some plants
animal.habitat: Rocky and sandy bottoms from the shallows to about 480 m, mostly at 4–50 m
animal.lifespan: Estimated to exceed 100 years in large individuals
animal.size: Commonly 25–50 cm long; record about 20 kg
animal.behaviour: Females carry thousands of eggs under the tail for about a year before they hatch.
fieldMarks: Dark greenish-brown to bluish shell, turning red only when cooked
Two large, unequal claws
Long, reddish antennae
Fan-shaped tail
animal.lookalikes: European lobster (Homarus gammarus) is bluer and lacks the spine on the underside of the rostrum. Caribbean spiny lobster (Panulirus argus) has no big claws and a spiny shell.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky coasts of the Gulf of Maine and Maritime Canada; lobster boats and pounds in Maine and Nova Scotia.
animal.season: Year-round; moves inshore and moults in summer

edibleParts: tail, claw and leg meat; tomalley and roe
edibilityNote: Usually boiled or steamed. The tomalley (digestive gland) can concentrate shellfish toxins during red tides, and authorities sometimes advise against eating it. Shellfish allergy is common.
lore: Early colonial accounts describe lobsters so abundant in New England that they were used as fish bait and fertiliser; only from the 19th century did canning and railways turn them into a luxury food.
funFact: About one lobster in a couple of million is bright blue because of a genetic mutation that alters its shell pigment protein.

summary: A small shrimp with one huge claw that snaps shut so fast it creates a collapsing bubble hot enough to emit a flash of light. The snap stuns prey and is one of the loudest sounds made by any animal.
nativeRange: Western Atlantic, from lower Chesapeake Bay and North Carolina to the Gulf of Mexico; Caribbean and Brazilian records are uncertain because the species was split into a complex
abilities: Claw snap produces a cavitation bubble that collapses with a sound above 200 dB (re 1 µPa at 1 m)
The collapsing bubble briefly reaches several thousand degrees and emits light ('shrimpoluminescence')
Can regrow a lost snapping claw, often switching which side carries it
Lives in mated pairs in burrows

animal.diet: Small fish, worms and crustaceans stunned by the snap
animal.habitat: Burrows and crevices in oyster reefs, rubble, seagrass and muddy estuaries
animal.behaviour: Rivals threaten each other by opening the snapping claw and firing water jets rather than fighting directly.
fieldMarks: Small, greenish to translucent brown shrimp
One massively enlarged claw, up to half the body length
Eyes hidden under a hood on the carapace
Crackling sound from reefs
animal.voice: A sharp click or pop; massed shrimp make a constant frying or crackling sound underwater.
animal.lookalikes: Other Alpheus and Synalpheus snapping shrimps are separated by claw shape and colour; Synalpheus are usually smaller and live inside sponges.
animal.whereToSee: Oyster reefs and estuaries of the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts; listen with a hydrophone or near docks at low tide.
animal.season: Year-round

lore: During the Second World War, the crackle of snapping shrimp beds interfered with naval sonar, and submarines were able to use the noise as acoustic cover.
funFact: Light flashes from its collapsing bubbles were first recorded in this species in 2001 and nicknamed 'shrimpoluminescence'.

summary: Not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised animals (zooids) that function as one organism, drifting on a gas-filled sail. Its tentacles, often around 10 m and sometimes far longer, deliver an extremely painful sting.
nativeRange: Warm and temperate waters of the Atlantic, drifting widely; Indo-Pacific 'bluebottles' are now generally treated as separate Physalia species
abilities: Colony of zooids specialised for floating, catching prey, digestion and reproduction
Inflates its float with gas including carbon monoxide
Sails can be angled left or right, so wind drives different individuals in different directions
Stinging cells remain active on stranded or dead specimens

animal.diet: Small fish and fish larvae, shrimp and other plankton caught on the tentacles
animal.habitat: Surface of the open ocean; washed ashore by onshore winds
animal.size: Float up to about 30 cm; tentacles commonly about 10 m, recorded to 30 m
animal.behaviour: Tentacles contract to pull paralysed prey up to digestive zooids beneath the float.
fieldMarks: Translucent, blue-violet, gas-filled float with a pink-edged crest
Long blue tentacles trailing below
Often stranded in rows along beaches after storms
No bell or pulsing swimming
animal.lookalikes: By-the-wind sailor (Velella velella) is a small, flat blue disc with a rigid diagonal sail and only short tentacles. Blue button (Porpita porpita) is a flat, round disc. Pacific bluebottles (Physalia utriculus) are smaller with a single main tentacle.
animal.whereToSee: Atlantic beaches of Florida, the Caribbean, the Canary Islands and occasionally Britain and Ireland after strong westerlies. Do not touch stranded ones: their tentacles still sting.
animal.season: Strandings follow onshore winds; Florida mostly winter, Europe often late summer–autumn

lore: Sailors named it after the Portuguese caravel or man-of-war, whose rounded sail its float resembles.
funFact: The blue sea slug (Glaucus atlanticus) eats man o' war tentacles and stores their unfired stinging cells in its own body for defence.

summary: A translucent, saucer-shaped jellyfish marked with four pale rings, the most familiar jellyfish of European coasts and public aquariums. Its life cycle alternates between a tiny polyp on the sea floor and the drifting medusa.
nativeRange: North-east Atlantic and adjacent seas; very similar moon jellies worldwide are now recognised as separate, cryptic Aurelia species
abilities: Polyps bud off stacks of baby jellyfish (strobilation) when water temperature changes
Blooms can contain millions of individuals and block power-station cooling intakes
Mild sting from short marginal tentacles

animal.diet: Plankton, fish eggs and larvae, caught in mucus on the bell and wiped to the mouth by oral arms
animal.habitat: Coastal waters, bays and harbours, often in sheltered, nutrient-rich water
animal.lifespan: Medusae usually a few months to a year; polyps can persist for years
animal.behaviour: Medusae drift and gently pulse near the surface; polyps attach to hard surfaces underneath piers and boats.
fieldMarks: Clear, flat, saucer-shaped bell
Four horseshoe-shaped rings (gonads), pale violet, pink or white
Short fringe of fine tentacles around the edge
Four frilly oral arms under the bell
animal.lookalikes: Compass jellyfish (Chrysaora hysoscella) has brown V-shaped markings radiating from the centre. Lion's mane (Cyanea capillata) is reddish-brown with a mass of long tentacles. Blue jellyfish (Cyanea lamarckii) is bluish with long tentacles.
animal.whereToSee: Harbours and bays around Britain, the North Sea and the Baltic in summer; public aquariums worldwide.
animal.season: Medusae mainly May–Sep in European waters

lore: Moon jellyfish polyps were flown into orbit aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1991 to study how gravity-sensing organs develop in microgravity.
funFact: Jellyfish raised in space had trouble swimming normally once back on Earth, apparently because their gravity sensors developed differently.

summary: The sea star that gave ecology the idea of the 'keystone species'. When Robert Paine removed it from rocks in Washington State in the 1960s, mussels took over and the variety of shore life collapsed.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from Alaska to Baja California
abilities: Pulls mussel shells apart with hundreds of tube feet
Pushes its stomach out through its mouth to digest prey inside the shell
Regenerates lost arms
Can survive hours out of water at low tide

animal.diet: Mainly California mussels; also barnacles, limpets, snails and chitons
animal.habitat: Wave-exposed rocky shores and mussel beds, from mid-intertidal to about 90 m
animal.size: Usually 10–25 cm across, up to about 50 cm
animal.behaviour: At high tide it moves up into mussel beds to feed; at low tide it clusters in crevices to avoid drying out.
fieldMarks: Five thick, stiff arms
Colour purple, orange, ochre or brown
Upper surface covered with small white spines in a net-like or star-shaped pattern
Firm, rough texture
animal.lookalikes: Giant spined star (Pisaster giganteus) has larger, blue-ringed spines. Mottled star (Evasterias troschelii) has slimmer arms and is mottled. Leather star (Dermasterias imbricata) is smooth and slippery.
animal.whereToSee: Rocky shores at low tide from Vancouver Island to California, e.g. Olympic National Park, Monterey Bay and Mukkaw Bay (Washington).
animal.season: Year-round; best seen on low spring tides

lore: Robert Paine's experiments at Mukkaw Bay, published in 1966 and 1969, coined the term 'keystone species', one of the most influential ideas in conservation biology.
funFact: Sea star wasting syndrome killed most ochre stars along parts of the Pacific coast in 2013–2014, turning the animals into melting, disintegrating masses; many populations have since partly recovered.

summary: A large, many-armed starfish covered in venomous spines that eats living coral. In population outbreaks it can strip whole reefs, and it is one of the main causes of coral loss on the Great Barrier Reef.
nativeRange: Tropical Pacific Ocean, from Japan and the Philippines through the Great Barrier Reef, Melanesia and Micronesia to Polynesia; other Acanthaster species replace it in the Indian Ocean and Red Sea
abilities: Eats coral by turning its stomach out over the colony and digesting the tissue
A large female can release tens of millions of eggs in a season
Spines contain saponins that cause painful, swelling wounds
Outbreak densities can reach many thousands per square kilometre

animal.diet: Living hard corals, preferring fast-growing table and branching Acropora
animal.habitat: Coral reefs, mostly at depths of a few metres to about 30 m
animal.size: Usually 25–35 cm across, sometimes over 50 cm
animal.behaviour: It feeds mostly at night and hides under coral during the day; feeding leaves bright white patches of dead coral skeleton.
fieldMarks: Large starfish with 7–23 arms
Upper surface covered with long, sharp spines
Colour grey-green, purple, red or blue
White feeding scars on nearby coral
animal.lookalikes: Other crown-of-thorns species (A. planci in the northern Indian Ocean, A. mauritiensis in the southern Indian Ocean, A. benziei in the Red Sea) are separated by range and genetics. No other reef starfish is as spiny.
animal.whereToSee: Reefs of the Great Barrier Reef, Okinawa, Guam and Fiji, particularly during outbreaks.
animal.season: Year-round; spawning in the warm season (about Dec–Feb on the Great Barrier Reef)

lore: A major outbreak was first reported at Green Island near Cairns in the early 1960s; reef managers now cull starfish by injecting them with vinegar or bile salts.
funFact: Its natural predators include the giant triton snail (Charonia tritonis), the humphead wrasse and the starry pufferfish, all reduced by fishing and shell collecting.

summary: A spiny purple urchin of North America's Pacific coast that, when its predators decline, can mow down kelp forests and leave bare 'urchin barrens'. It is also a classic laboratory animal for studying fertilisation and embryo development.
nativeRange: Pacific coast of North America from British Columbia (and parts of Alaska) to Baja California
abilities: Grinds algae and kelp with a five-toothed jaw called Aristotle's lantern
Bores pits into solid rock with its teeth and spines
Senses light with its tube feet, using its whole body as an eye
Can survive years of starvation in barrens in a dormant-like state
Some individuals live 50 years or more

animal.diet: Kelp and other algae, especially drift kelp
animal.habitat: Rocky shores and reefs from the low intertidal to about 160 m
animal.behaviour: When drift kelp is plentiful urchins hide in crevices; when it runs short they emerge and graze living kelp, sometimes creating barrens.
fieldMarks: Round, spiny urchin with dense, short, bright purple spines
Juveniles may be greenish
Often packed into rock pits it has bored itself
Tube feet extend between the spines
animal.lookalikes: Red sea urchin (Mesocentrotus franciscanus) is larger (to about 18 cm) with long red to maroon spines. Green urchin (S. droebachiensis) has greenish spines and lives mainly further north.
animal.whereToSee: Tide pools and kelp reefs from Oregon to southern California; dense barrens off Mendocino and Sonoma counties since 2014.
animal.season: Year-round

edibilityNote: The gonads are eaten raw as uni. Barrens urchins are often thin, so some ventures collect and 'ranch' them to fatten them for market while restoring kelp.
funFact: Its genome, sequenced in 2006, was the first of any echinoderm and revealed genes for vision-related proteins despite it having no eyes.

summary: A blood-feeding freshwater leech used in medicine for over two thousand years. Once collected in such numbers that it vanished from much of Europe, it is again used in hospitals to rescue reattached fingers and skin flaps.
nativeRange: Europe, from Britain and southern Scandinavia east to the Urals
abilities: Saliva contains hirudin, a powerful anticoagulant, plus anaesthetic and vessel-widening compounds
Three jaws with many tiny teeth leave a Y-shaped bite
Can take several times its own weight in blood in one meal
Can go months between meals

uses.use: Leeches cleared by the US FDA in 2004 as a medical device to relieve venous congestion in reattached digits and skin flaps
Bloodletting by leeches to rebalance the humours, at its peak in 19th-century France
Leech therapy (jalaukavacharana; irsal-e-alaq) for skin disease, abscesses and joint pain, using local leech species

medicinal.cautions: Use only under medical supervision: bites bleed for hours and can transmit Aeromonas bacterial infection, so patients usually receive preventive antibiotics. Wild collection is restricted under CITES and national laws.

animal.diet: Blood of amphibians, fish, birds and mammals; young leeches feed on frogs and tadpoles
animal.habitat: Warm, shallow, weedy ponds and marshes, often trampled by livestock
animal.size: About 10–12 cm when extended, up to about 20 cm
animal.behaviour: It senses ripples and warmth in the water and swims towards potential hosts with an undulating motion.
fieldMarks: Flattened, segmented, olive-green to brown body
Pair of reddish or orange stripes along the back broken by black spots
Spotted, greenish-yellow underside
Sucker at each end
animal.lookalikes: Mediterranean medicinal leech (Hirudo verbana), widely sold for medical use, differs in stripe pattern and has a plainer underside. Horse leech (Haemopis sanguisuga) is dull grey-brown and cannot bite through human skin.
animal.whereToSee: Rare; scattered ponds in Britain (e.g. Romney Marsh, New Forest, Lake District) and eastern Europe.
animal.season: Active in warm water, Jun–Sep

lore: The Old English word 'læce' meant both physician and leech. In the 1830s France imported tens of millions of leeches a year for bloodletting, emptying wetlands across Europe.
funFact: The anticoagulant drugs bivalirudin and lepirudin were developed from hirudin, the protein in leech saliva.

summary: A soft, velvety creature with stubby legs that hunts by squirting nets of sticky slime. It belongs to the Onychophora, an ancient group related to arthropods whose body plan resembles fossils from the Cambrian seas more than 500 million years ago.
nativeRange: South-eastern Australia, notably the cool forests of south-eastern New South Wales (e.g. Tallaganda State Forest)
abilities: Squirts sticky, protein-based slime from glands beside the mouth, entangling prey several centimetres away
Eats its own slime after a hunt to recycle the protein
Lives in social groups led by a dominant female that feeds first
Gives birth to live young

animal.diet: Crickets, spiders, woodlice and other small invertebrates
animal.habitat: Inside moist rotting logs in cool forest
animal.behaviour: Group members cooperate to subdue large prey; individuals recognise and are aggressive towards velvet worms from other groups.
fieldMarks: Soft, cylindrical body covered in tiny velvety papillae
Fifteen pairs of stubby, unjointed legs ending in small claws
One pair of ringed antennae
Dark blue-grey to brown with fine patterning
animal.lookalikes: Can be mistaken for a caterpillar or slug, but caterpillars have jointed true legs and slugs have none. Many other Australian velvet worm species differ in leg number, colour and range.
animal.whereToSee: Rotting logs in wet forest of south-eastern NSW; rarely seen in the open except on damp nights.
animal.season: Most active in cool, damp weather

lore: The first velvet worm known to science was described from St Vincent in 1826 by Lansdown Guilding, who thought it was a kind of slug.
funFact: Velvet worm slime turns from liquid into strong fibres as it is stretched, and can be dissolved and re-spun, which has inspired research into recyclable materials.

summary: A fist-sized land snail from East Africa that has spread across the tropics and is listed among the world's worst invasive species. It eats hundreds of plant species, can lay over a thousand eggs a year, and can carry rat lungworm, a parasite that causes meningitis.
nativeRange: Coastal East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique); invasive across South and Southeast Asia, the Pacific, the Caribbean and South America
abilities: Eats more than 500 kinds of plants, as well as plaster and concrete for calcium
Lays clutches of 100–400 eggs several times a year
Survives dry seasons by sealing its shell and becoming dormant for months
Hermaphrodite; can store sperm from a single mating for many months

animal.diet: Crops, garden plants, fallen fruit, decaying matter, and calcium from walls and shells
animal.habitat: Farms, gardens, plantations and disturbed land in warm, humid regions
animal.lifespan: Usually 3–5 years; up to about 9 years
animal.size: Shell typically 7–10 cm long, up to about 20 cm
animal.behaviour: Active at night and after rain; in dry periods it hides in soil or under debris, sealed behind a mucus membrane.
fieldMarks: Large, tall, cone-shaped shell
Brown to reddish-brown with darker vertical streaks
Seven to nine whorls
Grey-brown body with long tentacles
animal.lookalikes: Giant Ghana tiger snail (Achatina achatina) is larger with bold zig-zag stripes. Rosy wolfsnail (Euglandina rosea) is smaller, pinkish, and predatory. Native apple snails (Pomacea) live in water and have a rounder shell.
animal.whereToSee: Gardens and farmland across tropical Asia, Pacific islands and parts of Brazil; native forests of coastal Kenya and Tanzania.
animal.season: Most active in the rainy season

edibilityNote: Eaten in parts of Africa and Asia, but it can carry rat lungworm (Angiostrongylus cantonensis), which causes eosinophilic meningitis. Must be cooked thoroughly; never eat raw, and wash hands after handling.
lore: It was carried from East Africa to Mauritius in the early 1800s and to India by the 1840s, then across Asia and the Pacific; in Florida a boy's three pet snails brought from Hawaii in 1966 led to a decade-long eradication campaign.
funFact: The rosy wolfsnail introduced to Pacific islands to eat it instead wiped out dozens of native Partula tree snails, a famous biological-control disaster.
